utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Concluding the witness Mr. Candic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are in the summary before the Court at paragraph 21.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Candic, a couple of -- or a few matters of detail before we conclude. During the battle for Vukovar in the autumn of 1991, did you become aware of a JNA soldier arrested by his commanding officer for executing four Croat civilians who was brought to the Central KOG in Zemun near Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do know that during the fall of Vukovar or, rather, when Vukovar was won over by the JNA, a soldier from the traffic unit of the Batajnica air force garrison who was transferring detained civilians to Serbia, when an attempt was made for this transport to be effected into Serbia, the soldier -- rather, he wasn't a soldier, he had two stripes on his shoulders, a lower rank -- he shot in the back, executing four civilians. He was a lance corporal, in fact. And the commander of his unit considered that this was contrary to the rules of international warfare, and this lance corporal was taken into custody and taken to the Central Intelligence Group for processing and further treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact and in the event, what processing was undertaken? How long did he stay in custody?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, that is to say when that soldier was brought in to the Central Counter-Intelligence Group in Zemun, he was taken over by Lieutenant Colonel Ratko Radakovic, and he talked to him, he interrogated him for an hour, no more than that, but the talk was not fruitful. It did not provide documents which would be handed over to the investigating judge or, rather, the prosecutor later on to bring him to accountability and take proceedings against him. This interrogation, I would say, took the form of a leisurely conversation in a relaxed mood, and one hour later, that soldier was released from the Central Counter-Intelligence Group, and of course he himself took the bus, the town bus, to his unit. So actually, nothing was done with respect to the criminal liability of that particular soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And did that colonel, Colonel Ratko Radakovic, express a view on the gravity of the killings of this sort to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions I just peeped through the door of the room in which the conversation was taking place. And it wasn't Colonel Ratko Radakovic, it was Lieutenant Colonel Ratko Radakovic. And once the soldier was released, I asked him why he had let him go because he had killed four people, shooting them in the back. And all he said to me by way of response was, "Well, it happens. It happens every day and there's nothing we can really do about it for each individual case. We can't file a criminal report for each case." And that to me, as a man, as a legalist, seemed to me to be something quite flagrant. And I couldn't believe that a high-ranking officer could behave in that way faced with a situation of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Candic, short accounts by you, please, of two named operations, one called Labrador and one called Opera. Let's start with Labrador. Can you give us in literally two, three, four sentences your account of what Labrador was.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operation Opera or, rather, the operative undertaking called Opera was the natural continuation of the operation called Labrador. In Zagreb, what happened was a network was set up for a strong one among the members of the state security of the state of Croatia and high-ranking officials within the HDZ party, and it was within this operation Labrador that several concrete operations were undertaken, terrorist acts in actual fact, and when the Croatian authorities learnt of an operation of this kind in Zagreb, they -- the members of Operation Labrador fled to Belgrade with all the documents. Upon their arrival in Belgrade, which means in the second half of August, a department was set up for a propaganda war, propaganda warfare, and that was named Opera for short, and its headquarters were located in the aviation centre near the command of the air force and anti-air defence department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A couple of points of detail. The first point of detail may or may not relate to either of these operations. Was there action at the Jewish graves at a cemetery in Zagreb connected to either of these named operations?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is true that within Operation Labrador, or, rather, when this network of collaborators was active in Zagreb, at the Mirogoj cemetery in Zagreb, a terrorist attack was launched and Jewish graves were mined at the Mirogoj cemetery, the object being that the Croatian authorities should be represented and shown as being pro-fascist or, rather, to create animosity, that the Jews should have animosity towards the Croatian authorities in Zagreb. Another terrorist act was also being planned on the synagogue in Zagreb. However, that was never carried out because the members of the Labrador operation had to flee to Belgrade because they were in danger of being arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally on Labrador, who was the officer in charge of Labrador and what, if any, part of the KOG detachments were involved or was involved?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officer in charge for Operation Labrador was the head of the security department, Slobodan Rakocevic, in Zemun, while the operative staff of the second detachment of the counter-intelligence group in Zagreb, first and foremost Colonel Ivan Sabolovic and Major Cedo Knezevic, were the people who had links with the collaborators in Zagreb and the persons in the field in the state security that actually launched these operations and sent in reports about everything that was happening in Zagreb and in the top leadership of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is "Labrador" the name of a place or does it have any special meaning in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it may be the name of a place, but let's see from the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us, Mr. Candic? Does the name "Labrador" relate to a place? Why was the name chosen for this particular operation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every undertaking secret code names are ascribed which are then used in all correspondence and links between the superiors and their subordinates in the security services. In this case, the operation was given the secret name of Labrador in -- to associate -- to bring to mind the breed of dog that is called Labrador because the collaborators in Zagreb and in the region further afield set up in several locations explosives, weapons, and everything they needed for performing further terrorist acts in Zagreb and further afield as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then let's ask the same question in relation to the next operation, Opera. Was there any particular reason for that word being used for the second operation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "Opera" is once again short for the department for propaganda warfare which is a higher level from the Operation Labrador, being a retriever, and it was to serve for psychological and propaganda activity throughout the territory of the Republic of Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Serbia as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now give us a few particular examples of the Opera operation in action? First in relation to propaganda, disinformation, and ethnic unrest, what sort of things were done?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when speaking of Opera, let me first say that one of the main actors in the Opera operation, Radenko Radojcic, informed me that detailed, specific plans were devised for the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina within this Operation Opera, first of all for the Republic of Croatia and then for Bosnia-Herzegovina. And he was the one who told me - and I was a witness to this - about several of these actions that were undertaken and effected within Operation Opera. And let me mention by way of an example one particular operation which had as its goal to show the Croatian authorities up as being fascist, because in Serbia and along the borders with Croatia, there were quite a lot of Croats, Croats living in Serbia, that is, on the Serbian side of the border, and they were terrorised daily by the volunteer units belonging to Seselj, Arkan, and the Jovic bothers from Pasova. So what they did was to throw in bombs into their yards, and they were intimidated and frightened in that way, and many of them fled into Croatia. And they would have it appear as if nobody was actually making them flee. And in order to prove this point, an operation was undertaken in the central part of the television news bulletin in Belgrade where a conversation was televised between two leaders of the HDZ. One leader represented himself as being from -- an HDZ leader from Zagreb, and the other man was a leader from Ilok, HDZ leader from Ilok. I saw that news bulletin on television, and I recognised the voices. I knew that these two men, these two HDZ prominent officials were Radenko Radojcic on the one hand and, on the other, Lieutenant Colonel Ivan Sabolovic. I recognised their voices. The leader of the HDZ from Zagreb issued an order to the other man, the man from Ilok, HDZ man from Ilok, to mobilise the entire Croatian population in Serbia, that is to say along the borders with Croatia, and that within the space of two days that they should move towards Zagreb. The HDZ man from Ilok in that conversation says that that is impossible, that it will be very difficult to do that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt. It's very difficult to follow this. Can we summarise it in a few words, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was what was being presented on the television accurate or was it disinformation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, it was disinformation, and the conversation between these two people was devised in advance. Lieutenant Colonel Radojcic and the other man, and they wanted to present it as being reality, portraying these as being the true leaders of the HDZ from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the purpose of it was to create what state of mind in the listeners?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the object, the whole object of this was that the viewers and the people in Serbia, first and foremost, would gain the impression that the Croatian authorities were fascist and that they wanted to have ethnically pure areas inhabited only by Croats and areas where the Serbs would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second category of example of Opera operation may relate to wire taps. Can you give us one or possibly two examples of that, but again explain in summary what happened and the purpose of what was done.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Opera had a wide range of technical devices for tapping, and everything was available to them. And they were able to rig Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. conversations, wiretap them in accordance with the plans that were made for Croatia and for Bosnia-Herzegovina and so on. And this was always linked to the propaganda that they wanted to disseminate, something that was read about with something that had taken place in the field within the frameworks of terrorist action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us one example, perhaps, of a rigged wiretap conversation and tell us what its true purpose was.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a concrete specific example was wire taps of conversations, yes, and there was an example of a conversation between Mile Dedakovic, known as Jastreb, the defender of Vukovar, and General Anton Tus in Zagreb. That was one example. On the basis of the wire taps - they intercepted conversations on several occasions between these two men - a conversation was compiled using excerpts from all these conversations in which Mile Dedakovic, Jastreb, asks for his assistance in weaponry, and he says to him that he mustn't count on any kind of assistance and that he was left to his own devices, he had to fend for himself and do as best as he could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Finally on Opera, was it the same unit, that is the unit of the 2nd KOG detachment that was involved, and if so, can you tell us about an incident on the railroad at Vinkovci?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what actually happened on that railroad at Vinkovci, but Radenko Radojcic told me, and he was very pleased when he told me this, that within the frameworks of Operation Opera or Plan Opera, that a terrorist action was effected along the railway line near Vinkovci, and a name was used there of the late president of the Croatian republic, Franjo Tudjman. The object of that operation was to show that this had come from Tudjman's orders and that this was to make Tudjman make official denials of that. And this is in fact what President Tudjman did on two occasions. And that is why Radenko Radojcic was so pleased and said that they had managed to achieve their objective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just yes or no: Was it still the 2nd KOG detachment that was involved in Opera or was it another detachment?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operation Opera was the 2nd Detachment of the counter-intelligence group from Zagreb with its men, Lieutenant Colonel Ivan Sabolovic, Radenko Radojcic as a collaborator from the Labrador operation who came to Belgrade, then there was Slavko Malobabic who was also a collaborator of the 2nd Detachment. So they were the main actors in Operation Opera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Staying just very briefly with propaganda, paragraph 24, you told us when you were last giving evidence about the Operation Proboj 2. Did officers involved in that operation engage in propaganda and disinformation activities via photographs of apparent war victims from Croatian villages?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I did talk about Proboj 2 and Major Ljuban Karan was at the head of it with a team of men, and they were in Eastern Slavonia and Ivica Katancic was with them from the technical department of the central counter-Intelligence group, and he always took with him a camera and an automatic rifle because that's where he fought. On several occasions, Ivica Katancic took the films with mutilated bodies to -- he brought them to the counter-intelligence group to show us the footage he had made and to show us what the Croats were doing to the Serbs in that part of Eastern Slavonia. And they were really terrible, dreadful pictures, dreadful footage. And some of those videotapes I showed -- played on Television Belgrade. And I recognised these images and the footage taken by Katancic in the area of Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the event, were you clear what the ethnic origin of the victims shown was?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, what Ivica Katancic said and Karan said, that the victims were Serbs, to me as an officer this didn't seem to be quite logical. It wasn't logical that the Croats should carry out this massacre and slaughter in a particular area and to leave the area that they had won over, for Ivica Katancic to be able to come in and take films of that and take the footage back to Belgrade. I think what happened was quite the reverse; that the victims were Croats, in fact, and they were depicted as being Serb victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've already dealt, I think, last time with paragraph 27, the witness having testified about Vasiljevic's report of Milosevic asking the generals to sign a loyalty oath. Just one detail in case this didn't emerge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Candic, you did give an account on the last occasion of that request by the accused Milosevic that generals should sign a loyalty oath. According to Vasiljevic, did any or many of the generals sign such an oath?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talked about what General Vasiljevic informed us of, the head of the security department, that certain generals were signing loyalty oaths to Slobodan Milosevic, he mentioned a particular name and he said, "Your General Stevanovic, nicknamed Mika Sprajc, is one of them, one of the people who signed this loyalty oath to Slobodan Milosevic." And he was the commander of the 1st Airborne Corps in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time this request was made by the accused, did the accused have any authority in the form of membership of the Presidency or the Supreme Command to make such a request of the generals?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this was going on, the accused had no right to ask the generals or anybody else, any other officers for that matter, to sign a loyalty oath because the Supreme Command of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, they had the Presidency as the supreme organ and not the President of Serbia, in this case the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Candic, you left the JNA in February 1992. Did you do so of your own free will?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I left of my own free well. Because for a relatively long period of time this dissatisfaction in me had been mounting. And so when it -- I had had enough, I decided to leave on the 19th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Wait there, you will be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Candic, since you're talking about the state of affairs in the JNA as it was until you left it, tell me, was there any discrimination in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I was leaving the JNA, I must be honest, there was no discrimination against me, at any rate. I enjoyed authority and the trust of the people I was working with. I can say, however, that there was discrimination against the Croats who were leaving the army at the time. And at the time when the war in Croatia began, they were trying to desert, in a way, on one hand. Some of them who were caught before they actually deserted were brought for interrogation to the Central Counter-Intelligence Group, exhaustive interviews were conducted with them. They were first threatened with prison and charges of desertion, whereas the ultimate aim was to recruit them as collaborators of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During all the time that you were in the JNA, and that was several years, was there any discrimination based on ethnicity in the ranks?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I spent a long time in the service of the JNA, and I've made an oath here to tell the truth and only the truth, and I can say that with the exception of that year, 1991 and the beginning of 1992, there was no discrimination of any kind except against ethnic Albanians in the JNA. Large-scale operative processing was conducted against them to ascertain that they were not working for the Albanian side, and sometimes these investigations were based on false assumptions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that there was discrimination against officers who were deserting from the JNA, tell me, how can that be discrimination if somebody had decided to leave the army, to desert? Was that a move initiated by the person who had decided to desert or was somebody expelling them from the army?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a moral decision made by every individual. I must tell you one truth here - and that's what I'm supposed to do - the people who were -- who wished to leave the army were called deserters, but nobody ever raised the issue of the withdrawal of the JNA from Slovenia, where after the brief war that took place there, the government of Slovenia decided that the JNA should be withdrawn from Slovenia within three years, and that caused confusion in the Presidency in Belgrade which held long sessions. These sessions ended with Borisav Jovic, the president, requesting from the Federal Secretary of Defence, Veljko Kadijevic, to make the decision himself and the latter took out a paper and said since the people don't want us in Slovenia any more, I suggest that the army withdraw within three months. Therefore, I don't see why a Croat should be called a deserter if such a decision had been made already at that time by the Presidency and the federal secretary himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that decision concerned the withdrawal of army from Slovenia, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereas desertion of Croatian officers from the JNA was not related to Slovenia. It was related to Croatia. And you, as a counter-intelligence officer, were following events in Croatia in 1990 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with it. I know a lot about it. It's not only about Slovenia. It's -- it was also about Macedonia. The Yugoslav Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. People's Army withdrew from there very easily. They had no longer any interest in that republic. It was no longer the country that we, the officers, made the oath to defend from Djevdjelija to Mount Triglav.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about Croatia, Mr. Candic. What was going on in Croatia in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that as well as I do. It was the log revolution and all the things that were going on in relation to the insurgence of Serbs in the Republic of Croatia and the involvement of the JNA, which intensely helped them, primarily with air force units using rockets and other equipment. It was not the job of the JNA to do this within their own country. They were supposed to defend their country from the enemy without.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems from what you told us that your job in the army did not actually involve many of the things that you were doing.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were doing the things that were in our job description, but it was other people, including you, who made many other things happen in all of Yugoslavia and Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know that, but I'm asking you about your testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please ask a specific question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll stick to what you said. You said, among other things, that in 1989, 1990, 1991, you were creating a network of informers in all areas, all spheres of society.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your main targets were government agencies, the media, businesses, schools; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But although you targeted all spheres of society, your main targets were government agencies and the police force.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in response to a question whether it was linked to ethnicity, you answered that your activities did not take into account ethnicity, and you aimed at the largest possible coverage.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said we did that in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. And in 1990 and 1991, your main targets were civilians and not the Ministry of the Interior or security services. You said that you had your own informers within security services themselves and within the police force itself.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. I said we tried to recruit collaborators within the security services of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, not Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but you were obviously doing something illegal over this entire period. Tell me, please, how many people were employed in this security service you -- where you worked?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I worked. Let me answer first the first part of your question about the illegality of our work. I already said that we were doing this against the law, but that was the instruction we had been given. The place where I worked, the counter-intelligence group, employed 37 people. That was the counter-intelligence group of the air force and air defence, plus services in Zagreb and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all of these units taken into account, how many people were employed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said 37.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thirty-seven plus?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can add another 15, so that makes a total of about 50 if we're talking about the counter-intelligence group, in addition to security services within units, namely assistant commanders for security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But however, the security services within units in the form of assistant commanders for security, they did not engage in this penetration of civilian structures. You did that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were 50 all in all.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how could 50 of you penetrate all civilian structures in half the country practically?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you how. I explained how it was only in the air defence and air force we were 50 of us, 50 members of the counter-intelligence group. However, in the army, in the navy, there were also counter-intelligence groups which numbered approximately the same number of people as in the air force. So if you take into account the fact that there were four armies, 1st, 3rd, 5th, and 7th, plus the navy, do your own arithmetics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About 200 people.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many more?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two hundred fifty. I would rather say 300.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So 300 of you created a network in all spheres of life, as you said; the police force, state administration, security services, education, government agencies, civilian structures, and so on. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am. I personally, as I said, or I did the last time, I had eight informers in members of security services that I recruited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't go into how many informers others were running, because I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you said yourself that your work was illegal but it was on orders --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- when orders are issued to officers, they're accompanied by explanations usually. What was the purpose of those activities? Were you preparing a military putsch if you were penetrating civilian structures like that? What was the objective?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had been informed that Yugoslavia was about to fall apart, to disintegrate, that that the leadership of Serbia and the security services were involved. And for the sake of preserving Yugoslavia we got these orders that we got.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it mean that you were working against the security services of the Republic of Serbia and the state leadership of Serbia with these orders?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not. We were not acting against the leadership or the security services of Serbia. You may have got such a report based on what Rakocevic said, that there is an Academy of Arts and Sciences in Belgrade which had prepared a document called the memorandum, that you were pulling the strings in all that. One of our operations officers taped this conversation, handed it over to a security officer, and after that, Colonel Slobodan Rakocevic was arrested and tried because you thought he was preparing a military putsch against you together with Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain, then, because it sounds contradictory to me. On one hand there are claims that I was controlling the army. On the other hand, you are telling us here that the army or, rather, the security services of the army were trying to control me. The two don't go together. Which is true?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you which is true. The truth is that the Yugoslav People's Army was trying to assume the role of the last cohesive factor for the preservation of the former Yugoslavia. Another truth is that the State Security Service, which you led, the police force of Serbia, and the reserve police force of Serbia, that was built up to such an extent that it was a match for the army at the time, both in terms of manpower and equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You obviously don't know what you're talking about, but I don't want to question you about things you know nothing about. I want to question about you about your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. You say he doesn't know what's talking about. You've heard that suggestion, Mr. Candic. Would you like to answer it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All this time I've been trying to tell you about things I know. The accused is trying to say that I don't know what I'm talking about. I really can't say anything about things I'm not familiar with. However, if I know something and if I'm certain of it, I'll say so. The State Security Service of Serbia was geared all the time at implementing the memorandum and creating a Greater Serbia, or the Rump Yugoslavia as it was called then popularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Candic. Let us be precise. You said during examination-in-chief that it was I who initiated the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Sciences, that I was pulling the strings, and the concept was about Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say you initiated the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences. I said that it was members of the Academy themselves who launched this memorandum, whereas you wanted this project to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I understood you as saying that I was the prime mover of the memorandum, of the whole project.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I said that you wanted it implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know when the memorandum was adopted?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I know; in 1986.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was adopted in 1984.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1986. Am I right, 1986?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course you're not right. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is a factual issue. You don't have to argue or repeat. Tell me, Mr. Candic, where did you read in this memorandum about Greater Serbia, disintegration or destruction of Yugoslavia? Where did you find in it any ambition to work against other nations within Yugoslavia? Where did you read that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the memorandum. It's true that there is nothing in it that explicitly talks about the creation of Greater Serbia, but there are chapters, such as the first chapter, that deals with the crisis in the former Yugoslavia that was evident at the time. The second chapter talks about the position and status of the Serbs as the most numerous nation within Yugoslavia, that accounted for about half of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us not waste time on this recounting of the contents. I asked you where you found Greater Serbia in the memorandum. Where did you find those ideas that seemed to go against any nation, any ethnic group in Yugoslavia? Can you tell me one single position of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1986 was a long time ago. I cannot quote anything, but I remember what the memorandum said about the Serbian people and how it was in jeopardy and how that had to be dealt with, and you could easily draw your own conclusions about the ultimate aim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the explanation that was commonly accepted in the army about the ultimate aim?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Small wonder, then, that you engaged in this broadcasting of videotapes on television created by your services.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tapes that I mentioned about crimes and the rest brought by Katancic Ivica had not been given by Opera, the propaganda war within the air force. They had been given to us by the State Security Service, by people from the counter-intelligence group who had been recruited by the State Security Service of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Candic, do you at least remember that these tapes dealing with the import of arms, about Spegelj and the rest, were broadcast on television and we were all shocked to see them as material taped by military services and they were broadcast on a decision by military authorities to familiarise the people with what was going on. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well the tapes that were shown on television in end 1990 beginning 1991 concerning Martin Spegelj, arms, imports, the role of Franjo Tudjman, president of the Republic of Croatia, and all that, the role of Gojko Susak and other protagonists. It is true that it was broadcast according to a decision of the military leadership but nothing was done by the Presidency to hold anyone criminally responsible. Who could have prevented this? The JNA couldn't. It was only the Supreme Command that could have done something about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Candic, do you remember that we all criticized the army at the time for engaging in showing images about violations of the law instead of protecting the border, confiscating, arresting people who were smuggling arms, which it was their duty to do?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how it should have been, but I do know that after this video was aired, fear spread even within the top leadership of Croatia and that President Tudjman himself that night had a fever, but he felt relieved when he received an answer from Belgrade that nothing would be done, and probably somebody had wanted it to be like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the army didn't want to do what it should have done by constitution but simply expected the public to respond to quite obvious violations of the law, very extreme violations. Is that what you're telling us? Did you have an explanation, you in the security service, why the army was not reacting in accordance with the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army would have acted if it had received orders from the Supreme Command, and it is quite clear that the Supreme Command or, rather, the Presidency, didn't want to do any such thing. If they had wanted it, the army would have followed those orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Candic. Let's go back to the beginning of your testimony here, because it is highly contradictory. You have been saying that you were in control of what was happening in Serbia, and yet on the other hand you're saying that the leadership of Serbia and I personally were in control of the army. So explain to me, please, whether you had ever, apart from what you've been talking about here, had you ever heard that any officer of the JNA had ever been asked to sign an oath of loyalty to me? Was what you had heard a provocation in your service or do you really believe in such a fabrication?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd ask you, first of all, not to distort my words. Never for a moment, and I am repeating myself, did I say that we controlled what was happening in Serbia. What I said was that we were criticised to the effect that we are not informed only about what was happening in Belgrade. So we did not control the situation there. As for this signing of an oath of loyalty in the federal Secretariat for National Defence, as well as in all units, the security bodies had their collaborators, which was normal. The information that Aleksandar Vasiljevic, the general, obtained that individual generals were signing loyalty to you is certainly information which he received from trusted collaborators. Maybe not from one collaborator but several of them who did not wish to sign such a loyalty oath to you. And that is what I referred to. I personally did not have such an occasion, nor was I of an appropriate rank to be present when somebody was signing or not signing loyalty to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Candic, do you remember that since we supported Yugoslavia, that is we Serbia, its political leadership and all the citizens considered the Yugoslav People's Army to be the legitimate armed force of Yugoslavia? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then why would we ask the legitimate armed forces of Yugoslavia, which we recognise and trust, select certain individuals to sign an oath of loyalty? Don't you know that that is quite the opposite?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, he can't answer why you should have done something, what your motives may have been. All he can say is what he knows of his own knowledge and observation. Now, frame the question differently.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I wish to draw your attention to a phenomenon, and that is that various witnesses have a piece of a mosaic fitted into their statements which is quite the reverse to what was actually happening. The previous witness was claiming here that in Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is your case. If you say that this witness has made it up or somebody has told him to say it, then you can put it to the witness and he can answer it, but it's no good asking him what may have been going on in your mind at the time. He doesn't know. Well, let's deal with it. What the accused is putting to you, Mr. Candic, is this: That you've had, it's said, evidence fitted in as part of a mosaic. So what in effect is being said is that you've been told or somebody's suggested that you should say something, apparently this point about the oath of loyalty. Has anybody suggested that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I uttered a single word as part of my testimony, I read out loud the solemn declaration that I would tell the truth and nothing but the truth. No person can be born in this world who can tell me, "Say such-and-such a thing" if it's something I don't know. So there is no human being on this earth who could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Candic. Let me hold you to your word then. So you know, because you said you wouldn't say anything that you don't know, so you do know that some generals signed an oath of loyalty to me. You know that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that General Aleksandar Vasiljevic informed us that some generals had signed an oath of loyalty to you, had signed it. Among them, he said, was one of your generals, that is he meant an air force general, General Stevanovic, nicknamed Mika Sprajc, the commander of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he then explain to you when he informed you about it what that oath looked like, this oath of the loyalty, what the words were, et cetera? Do you have any kind of knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't go into such details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, tell me, Mr. Candic, since you're a professional security -- intelligence officer, could you believe such nonsense that the president of a republic that was a component part of Yugoslavia would ask generals to sign oaths of loyalty to him, generals of the JNA, over which he has absolute no authority? Did that seem probable to you or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had known General Aleksandar Vasiljevic for about ten years, and what he said I accepted without any doubt, and I thought it would be -- it must be 100 per cent true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was common knowledge that it was in Croatia that generals were required to leave the JNA and to sign loyalty over there and that Izetbegovic had asked his own to abandon the JNA and to sign loyalty to them over there. We didn't ask anyone to leave the JNA. We supported the JNA. Do you -- are you aware of these phenomena in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to Croatia, I am familiar with such events, but these were public calls to the officers. When the war had started in the Republic of Croatia, there was a public call to the officers to abandon the JNA and to join the defence forces of the Republic of Croatia. When Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it comes to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, President Izetbegovic, he did not ask an oath of loyalty to be signed to him. President Izetbegovic, even at a point in time before the war in Bosnia had started, had made suggestions that the Yugoslav People's Army should remain as an armed force such as it was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a defensive force for Bosnia-Herzegovina without any changes having to be made such as it was at that time. But this was not accepted in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That again is not true, but never mind. Tell me, when did Izetbegovic call? The last time you testified here, you said that Izetbegovic had called on the Muslims and the Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina who had been members of the JNA to abandon the JNA, and when a mobilisation call was made, that they should not respond. Is that what you said? Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to intervene for a third time. Do not distort my words. Never did I say that Izetbegovic was calling on members of the JNA to abandon the JNA. What I had said was that the President Izetbegovic had called on the reservists not to respond to the mobilisation call. This was made in public, addressed to Croats and Muslims but not to the officers of the JNA, that is, the active-duty officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Candic, I took note of this. It is not my intention to distort your words. You can find this in the transcript. Izetbegovic called on them not to -- to the Bosniaks and Croats, not to respond. That is the terms you used. And those who had responded, to return home. That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say a part of what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no point in arguing about this. We can look at the transcript in due course. Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wish to ask a question in this connection. Did you say that they shouldn't respond and that those who did respond should return home? Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said with respect to those who had been called up from the reservists to be given wartime assignments - I was referring to them - and that those who had responded should return home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we don't have to check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I now find it. Has -- what the witness said was they were mobilised as reservists and received weapons since Izetbegovic appealed to Muslims and Croats not to respond. Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And then he went on to say that those who had responded should return home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Candic, you said, and I assume you can find that in the transcript too, what you said in the seat you're sitting in, that you wrote about everything, about the arming of all three groupings. I'm talking about Bosnia and Herzegovina now. The arming of the SDS, of the SDA, and the HDZ. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since you mentioned the arming of Serbs very briefly, tell me, what did you write about the arming of the SDA and the HDZ and what you knew about the arming of these two, that is the SDA and the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall be brief in answer to that question. With regard to the arming of the SDA, what I wrote about could be reduced to really minimal figures about smuggled weapons by individuals from the Republic of Croatia or Slovenia into Bosnia-Herzegovina in the boots of passenger cars; a few rifles. That's what I reported about, the people who were doing it and when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Never mind. We'll come to that. You were working in the department for internal enemies, that is, all those who were a threat to the constitutional order of Yugoslavia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those threats against the Yugoslav state, were they the -- the product of the imagination of the state security in the JNA or did they really exist?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to those threats, and once again I must specify the time period, threats against the constitutional order of the former Yugoslavia were real threats, and we took them very seriously. In a later stage, this was not legally regulated because one didn't know whether these were threats or whether it was a grouping or an ethnic group who were preparing not to experience a debacle as, unfortunately, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that as a high-ranking intelligence officer, you must have known that between 1981 and 1987, that is prior to all these events, that is up to 1987, 216 illegal groups had been discovered in the JNA, and then from 1987 to 1991, another 140 such groups, the aim of which was first to break up Yugoslavia, the JNA as a cohesive factor. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with that. I don't know whether the figure was 260, but certainly a large number of them. Up to 1987 and of course after that period, as you said. But really, I couldn't tell you what the exact figure was, but there were really very many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not familiar with any details about this?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were mostly groups acting from positions of Albanian nationalism and separatism, and a couple, one or two, that acted from positions of Croatian nationalism. There wasn't a single group that was discovered acting from positions of Greater Serbian nationalism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There wasn't single group acting from positions of Albanian national -- of Muslim nationalism?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The groups that you're talking about, so from those positions then, were they in favour of terrorist actions in the SFRY territory of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the groups which were discovered, as an example in the Zlata operation, Zlata 1 and 2 which was waged at a federal level, this was a group of Albanian nationalist and separatists, and they were tied up with members of the JNA and Albanian civilians, there were intentions within their plans to perform terrorist operations both within the JNA and of course within the civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were responsible for the Kosovo area and for the 90 municipalities in the northeast of Bosnia as well, which elements in Kosovo represented a threat to the constitutional order of Yugoslavia? Tell us that, then.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the main elements that were a threat to the constitutional order of Yugoslavia and -- was the attempts made to separate Kosovo from Yugoslavia and join it up with Albania. That was the main segment of threat, to topple the constitutional order of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from that time, do you know about the illegal underground Albanian separatist organisation that was called the Movement for an Albanian Republic in the SFRY? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The abbreviation was the PASRY, and I even read the platform they compiled and how these cases were clarified later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that from that time, eight members of this Central Committee of theirs were active from outside the country, from aboard?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many there were abroad. I focused on the members who were active within the Yugoslav People's Army, and I do know that there were quite a number of them from Zagreb, Sarajevo, Ljubljana, so that those are the sections that I can talk about, whereas within the operative action linked to that part, there were the security services of Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia and Slovenia taking part so that the data about the civilians, those working from abroad, from outside the country, is something I really don't know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know at all anything about the Military Committee, to use the PASRY abbreviation that you mentioned, this movement for an Albanian socialist republic, do you know anything about the Military Committee of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't actually a Military Committee but a military organisation, along those lines, in order to achieve this Albanian socialist republic within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to establish within your service who the JNA officers were who were illegally included into that Military Committee?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we were able to establish that, and we processed them and they were brought to trial. Lawsuits were brought against them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that this group in -- way back in 1984, had planned the liquidation of workers in the Ministry of the Interior in Kosovo and Metohija and planting explosives in Gjakove and the thermoelectric power station of Obiliq? Do you remember information along those lines?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but if you have any questions with respect to my testimony, ask me that. Don't go through my general knowledge. I really do know a great deal, but I do not want to talk about things that I have not brought up in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Candic, everything has to do with your testimony. Do you know Naim Maljoku and Azdemi Rahim? Do those names ring a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naim Maljoku was a captain, I think, in Lukavice. I don't know who this other man was. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rahim Azdemi was the other one. Were they members of this terrorist group?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members of this movement PASRY, the abbreviation was. That was what they were in favour of, and they were referred to as the Marxists and Leninists of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But regardless of the fact that these Albanian terrorists were united with respect to an ethnically purely Albanian state, were you aware at the time, and do you know today, that amongst themselves they were set up against the fascist traditions on the one hand, stemming from the Second World War, and their links with the German occupiers and the Italians and the representatives of this Marxist Leninist faction which come from the Albanian Enver Hoxha? Were you aware of that? Did you know about that? Did you have at your disposal that kind of analysis for the activities of this separatist organisation of theirs and those characteristics?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Working on the data available, we of course did take into account all the different segments, and we did not let a single detail slip through which could help us in our investigations in order to arrive at authentic and precise concrete responsibility and the linkage that existed or, rather, where a particular operation stemmed from in order to bring it to account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the mass exodus of Serbs from Kosovo and Metohija under pressure from these separatist organisations in Kosovo and Metohija over all those years, during the years that you worked there and when you were in charge of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was working in Kosovo, I did know and did hear about the exodus or, rather, attempt at an exodus, and the directive came from Belgrade that the Serbs from Kosovo should leave so that the impression should -- became that they were terrorised and forced to leave. That is not true. I was down there. I had my associates, both Serbs and Albanians, and I know exactly what was going on. There was an attempt to bring in the Romanians after what had happened in Romania, after the killing of Ceaucescu, to bring in Romanians into Kosovo and for Kosovo to become settled with Romanian inhabitants, to change the demographic composition of the Serbs and Albanians, the populace in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, come on, Mr. Candic. Now, how many Romanians came to Kosovo? Come on.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that a single Romanian came to Kosovo, but I did say that an attempt was made and that the offer was made to build houses for them as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, come on, Mr. Candic. As far as I remember, the Romanians were in Eastern Serbia, across the Danube, along the borders with Romania, and they engaged in trade. Some of them were refugees, but as for Kosovo, there were absolutely no Romanians there. Do you know that? Were you aware of that, Mr. Candic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that there were. I was just talking about an attempt to bring them in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Who wanted to bring them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leadership of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means me. You're trying to say that I wanted to bring in the Romanians into Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I was at the head of Serbia at that time. I have heard all sorts of things told in connection with my name, but never have I heard that I planned to bring in Romanians into Kosovo. Now, tell me, was part of your job to analyse the situation and foresee coming operations by hostile elements and the proposal of measures to thwart those attempts?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a component part of my daily job and the job of the state security organs in the JNA was to exert constant counter-intelligence assessments. And of course, within those assessments and evaluations we did incorporate all the elements required in intelligence work and assessment. And it was updated on a daily basis. So, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you must have known and been aware of the pressures exerted on the Serbs to leave the area. For example, a moment ago you claimed that a directive had come from Belgrade that the Serbs should leave the area. When did this direction come in?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was around the events of Azem Vllasi when he was arrested and what you said before, Azem Vllasi was taken into custody in the mine, when he was there with the miners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the directive then, that would be 1989, 1990, wouldn't it, for the Serbs to leave, to displace themselves. Do you know that it was at that time that public opinion and propaganda, et cetera, was precisely the reverse, that Serbs should not leave their homes but that those who had already left should go back, those who had left under pressure should go back to their villages and homes and to their own thresholds as the term was used at the day. Do you remember that, Mr. Candic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of Mitar Balevic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course I do, I do remember Mitar Balevic from Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, precisely. It was his sister-in-law, Ljilja Balevic, who told me about things of that kind taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what his sister-in-law told you about, what she spoke about, but when you're talking about 1990 or 1989, do you know how many Serbs under pressure left the area from 1980 to 1989, when you say the directive came?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nobody left. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. And what year were you in charge of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And up until 1989, you weren't in charge of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew nothing about the exodus of Serbs from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't delve into those problems. I had my units that I worked with, and I had to take care of the units I was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As you were working in your units, did any information ever reach you, any facts and figures, about the fact that the leadership of the JNA in any way whatsoever was in favour of any kind of Serb nationalism?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I was an organ of security within the units of the JNA up until 1988. Up until that year, I can safely say that I could not have felt - neither could anybody else, I think - feel any influence by any one of the republics or anybody from outside, wield influence on members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You said something that was quite right. The republics had no influence, wielded no authority or had any competence or were able to command the JNA; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I don't know whether I said that the republics didn't have it in their competence, but that was true. The republics didn't have the power to command the Yugoslav People's Army because it was a federal institution which was exclusively subordinated to the Supreme Command or, rather, the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was the collective supreme body; right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it the general position of your service, which as I have understood it was declared generally at your regular briefings, meetings, that the JNA was there to preserve Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This term was frequently used, that the JNA was the sole cohesive remaining factor - let me repeat it again - the sole cohesive factor for the preservation of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you share that opinion? Did you think that way too?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, then. You have presented one example according to which there was no information from Belgrade at a particular meeting you mentioned. Now I want to ask you this: Generally speaking, your service, did it collect information pertaining to the leadership of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but let me say that the system -- that the service is a system as was shown on the chart. So my part, the Central Counter-Intelligence Group, did not delve into matters of that kind, and that is why we were criticised, precisely for not doing anything along those lines. That is to say in Belgrade or in Serbia, to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you said that you attended a meeting at which General Vasiljevic explained that some generals, and you even said that I asked many generals, not only some but many generals, to sign an oath of loyalty, and you say that on page 4 of your statement, paragraph 4, tell me the names of the persons who attended that meeting apart from you and Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were members of the Central Counter-Intelligence Group, Lieutenant Colonel Radakovic, Colonel Tomislav -- Lieutenant Colonel Dzigurski, Karan Ljuban, Ivica Katancic, Dragan Grigorjevic [phoen], Branislav Nesic, Darvin Lisica, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, you say not only that I asked them to sign an oath of loyalty but that many generals did indeed do so.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that a portion of the generals did. I didn't say a large number. I didn't know how many. And we weren't told how many, what the exact figure was. But I was told that one of your generals did do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of my generals? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the -- in the air force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. From --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From your structures. From among your ranks. From your branch of the Armed Services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you believe, as you mentioned General Stevanovic; did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he at the time, the commander of what?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 1st Airborne Corps in Bajnica. The headquarters were at Bajnica, which means Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you claim that General Stevanovic signed an oath of loyalty to me.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I claim that, and it later proved to be correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did this prove to be correct later on?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it proved to be correct because there were constant demands from Eastern Slavonia for the air force to act in the area of Eastern Slavonia, that is to say, Vukovar and all the other places where the Croatian forces were deployed, and as such demands were thwarted by the commanders in the air force, Zvonko Jurjevic, who was a general at the time, the commander of the 1st Air Force Corps, Stevanovic, together with the commanders of the squadrons, at a meeting of the air force command that was held, they demonstratively got up and said, "My commanders, the commanders who are with me, let them stand up and leave." And all his commanders, the squadron commanders, got up, got to their feet, and left of the meeting that was led by the commander of the air force and air defence system of the air force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, what does that have to do with me? What is that to do with me or the Republic of Serbia, your relationships with the army and the JNA generally?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to discuss that matter, what it has to do with you. That's what you asked me and I gave you an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want us -- if you want us to take your answer into account, you must tell us how it affects the position. You were asked how it was proved to be correct that General Stevanovic signed the oath, and at the moment it is not clear from your answer how you say it was proved to be correct. Perhaps, Mr. Candic, you can explain and clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try and explain that once again. The commander of the air force corps, the 1st Airborne Corps in Belgrade, General Stevanovic, insisted nonstop that the air force and aviation units bomb the positions of the Croatian forces and towns in Eastern Slavonia or, rather, in the area of responsibility of the 1st Airborne Corps. As he was not allowed to do this by the commander of the air force, a meeting was held after these persistent demands were being made, and General Stevanovic attended the meeting, as did the commanders of the squadrons who were to have acted in Croatia, launched this attack. After hearing the explanation that the JNA could not behave in that way and could not attack a tower on some church, that the JNA was there to do other things, General Stevanovic demonstratively got up, got to his feet although he was the head of the air force, he was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've told us all that. What I want to understand is how it shows that he took the oath of loyalty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from what I said earlier on. The demands made for the Proboj 2 operation, that the Serbs should be armed. Major Ljuban Karan, parallel to the reports he sent through the regular channels to the security and intelligence department, drew up charts and diagrams that he sent to pilots at the Batajnica airport, saying which targets they should target, and he didn't inform Colonel Slobodan Rakocevic about that, which was the usual, regular channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've got to leave it there for the moment because it's time for the adjournment. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes. Mr. Candic, would you be back then. Mr. Milosevic, you can have up to an hour after the adjournment to complete your cross-examination, if you require it. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, from your legal officer, a few seconds ago I was informed that after the examination of this witness, we would be discussing matters related to the health of Mr. Milosevic. But as amici curiae, I believe we are duty-bound to draw your attention to the fact that, although I am not a cardiologist, I am not a psychiatrist or a doctor at all, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- noticed at the beginning of the examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are in the middle of an examination of witnesses. There is a matter which we wish to raise with Mr. Milosevic. We will do it in due course, and you will have a chance to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is my duty to draw your attention to this. A doctor hasn't been to see him in three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can do it in due course. Now, let us finish this examination, please. Mr. Milosevic, would you continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Candic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll rise for three minutes while it's dealt with. --- Break taken at 10.58 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Candic, based on the fact that the commander of the 1st Corps, as you say, quarreled with the commander of the air force at that meeting and walked out, you conclude that is the proof that he had signed loyalty to me. Is that it? Is that the proof for you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I didn't say it was proof. The proof is that Aleksandar Vasiljevic said that he had signed a loyalty oath. This only proves that he had departed from the line of command that was prescribed for the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, since, from what you say, General Vasiljevic allegedly made such serious accusations against me, how is it possible, then, that General Vasiljevic, as you said, ordered arms to be distributed to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who issued such orders. I only told you what I knew about Operations Proboj 1 and Proboj 2, and I said Aleksandar Vasiljevic was informed thereof. Who ordered that, I really don't know. And I don't know who the reports were copied to in addition to Vasiljevic. He wasn't the last in the line. These reports must have been submitted to some sort of political authority as well. I really wouldn't like to go into things I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But does it tell you something as an intelligence officer, as you explained yourself and as I would like to remind you, first you said that weapons were distributed up there in Western Bosnia from the depot of the Territorial Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said weapons were distributed from the depot of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. And then you described an event wherein an officer, whose rank I didn't note down, but it was an officer named Knezevic --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cedo Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Officer Cedo Knezevic was talking to Ljuban Karan, the latter complaining about the fact that the JNA was not giving them any weapons, and he said, "I have lots of that up there and I'll send you some."

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must quote again my own words. Major Ljuban Karan complained that Serbs in Eastern Slavonia were not armed and had no weapons. He didn't say that the JNA wouldn't give any weapons to Serbs. And it was after that that Cedo Knezevic said, "I have lots of it and I can give you some. Here is a friend of ours. He can confirm that I can arm half of the United States, if you want."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it speak then to the fact that weapons were distributed at that time according to old friendships, not on anybody's orders?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not so, because this operation had its name. It was Operation Proboj 1, Breakthrough 1. It's not something that somebody did of their own accord. They were following orders and reporting according to procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was this officer subordinated to, Cedo Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Cedo Knezevic was directly subordinated to, first of all, Colonel Tomislav Cuk head of the Central Counter-Intelligence Group, and since Colonel Cuk was directly linked with Slobodan Rakocevic, he was also subordinated to Slobodan Rakocevic, head of the security service of the air force and air defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just explained that precisely this Colonel Rakocevic, who, according to this chain of command, was the superior officer of Knezevic, was against this distribution of arms to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. And when those two trucks arrived in Zemun, Colonel Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Rakocevic spoke up against it. He said, "This can't be done this way.
