We have the JNA, and if anything is to be done, we have to receive orders first, and it is the JNA that should intervene rather than some volunteer units or paramilitary formations."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't it confirm that there were no orders to distribute weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you remember what I said, I said that Major Cedo Knezevic skipped one level in the chain of command. He went over the head of the head of the security service of the air force and air defence and addressed this precisely to the security administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that he had direct orders from General Vasiljevic to distribute weapons, going over the head of Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This General Vasiljevic that you mention made this accusation against me at that meeting, saying that I was requiring officers to sign loyalty oaths.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely how it was. He said that certain generals had to sign, and signed, loyalty oaths to you. And you keep using this term "General." You keep saying, "This general," as if you didn't know who he was. You arrested him and tried him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't arrest or try anyone, Mr. Candic, as you know well, nor did I have any authority over the JNA or the army of Yugoslavia until 1997. And after that time, I had authority over them because I was president of Yugoslavia. But let's move on. How do you explain, then, that orders came eventually if you say orders did not come from Vasiljevic? Rakocevic, who is in the chain of command, is against this. Knezevic, as you claim, distributes weapons according to somebody's orders. Whose orders?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I made my statement, when I testified here, Your Honours, I said that Cedo Knezevic was a deputy in the Proboj 1 operation, whereas the leader of the operation was Lieutenant Colonel Smiljanic from the 5th Army district, which means that the orders could have only been received by Lieutenant Colonel Smiljanic. I don't know from who. And according to those orders and the reporting chain, it must have been for this reason that the security service of the air defence and air force was skipped, bypassed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't it prove that it was somebody's arbitrary behaviour?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this operation was given a name, it means that it must have come from upstairs. So it couldn't have been arbitrary conduct. It was something intentional.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps this operation was given a name completely opposite to its nature. It was something designed to control the distribution of weapons, not to distribute weapons.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of orders were given exactly, but I said that weapons were distributed. It was not about controlling or monitoring the distribution of weapons. I even gave you a figure of how many weapons could have already been distributed at the moment when I became aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us dwell on one thing that you mentioned. You just mentioned Lieutenant Colonel Smiljanic. Is this the same person whose letter addressed to General Mladic was exhibited here?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I would like to hear your comment now on certain excerpts from this letter. He says towards the bottom of page 1: "Before the beginning of the war, I was head of the security service in the 9th Corps in Zagreb, and I was familiar with the origins of the rising Ustasha power. After my arrival in Plitvice, on the orders of my superiors, I had to stay in the territory of Krajina until the beginning of 1991." That's what it says here, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters don't have a copy and don't know where the accused is reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then he says, two pages later: "With the arrival of the notorious telegram which said that officers and soldiers born in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia should withdraw," that was after the approval of the Vance-Owen Plan to the effect that the army's withdrawing from the territory of the Serbian Krajina, and he says: "With the arrival of the notorious telegram that soldiers and officers born in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia should withdraw, the JNA remains composed of those born in Serbia and Montenegro. A large percentage was made up of active-duty officers and soldiers. They are made to leave from Bosnia and Herzegovina to Republika Srpska, whereas you Palestinians from the RSK can go to Nis or wherever you want. All those who are not from the territory of Yugoslavia or don't want to be involved can go wherever they like. I as a Palestinian --" I continue quoting -- "went to Knin, but I didn't desert as some people interpret that now. On leaving, I advised the officers who remained to keep a close watch on Second Lieutenant Kliko, a Muslim, because he would definitely desert to the Muslims, which unfortunately, happened since he deserted actually with a BOV." End of quote. This thing that you presented here as an exhibit, does it mean that the leadership of Yugoslavia abided by the Vance Plan and withdrew the JNA from the territory of the Serbian Krajina? Because that's exactly the event that he's describing.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not present or provide this letter. This is the first I hear of it. And second, what you quoted from this letter, I can only say that this is exactly how it happened. I was aware of certain things, such as that officers from Bosnia and Herzegovina were told to remain in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Officers from Croatia were told to remain in Croatia. But all of them were on the payroll in Belgrade until the last day of war and even after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How, then, do you explain this part where he says, "Those from Bosnia and Herzegovina should go to Republika Srpska, and you Palestinians from the RSK can go to Nis or wherever you like"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Smiljanic wanted to say, what he meant when he said he was a Palestinian. He was probably hurt by something that he was told in his communication with Ratko Mladic. I wouldn't like to comment on this. I'm also familiar with the Vance-Owen Plan, but it is not true that it was observed to the letter. All of the equipment and all of the personnel of the JNA remained in those areas where they had been deployed, and only those who were born in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia could, if they wanted to, to return. Some returned, but many remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the letter ought to be made available to the witness and indeed to the Prosecution and the other parties, not least because now it's been acknowledged as accurate in part by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where is the letter? I haven't got it, have I? Tab 3. Let the witness have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the English version, page 4, third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is your exhibit. I am not tendering it. You have tendered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness have his copy. Have you got it there, Mr. Candic, in a language you can follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at this letter, the one but last page of it. The ERN numbers are 72. The second paragraph, in which he says: "Attacks against the Serbian army of Krajina have -- are very arrogant and tested methods are being applied. Only some perpetrators have changed and it's at different times. Among others, enemies of the Republic of Serbia Krajina are ranked in the following manner as enemies of the Republic of Srpska Krajina." Then four dashes. "First the remnants of communism and the JNA on the territory of RSK. Secondly, the army of Yugoslavia. Thirdly, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the 5th Corps which is in their neighbourhood in Bosnian Krajina. And fourth, the army of the Republic of Croatia." Please explain to me how come that the army of Yugoslavia is being ranked as an enemy of the Republic of Serbian Krajina while at the same time it is alleged that the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was a component part of the army of Yugoslavia? Can you explain that for me, Mr. Candic? This is your exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: I didn't bring this letter, nor did I hand it over to the Prosecution or to the investigators. I saw this letter here. What the author of this letter meant in listing these elements, I really would rather not comment on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also consider that it wasn't the officers who distributed the weapons as it would emanate from the conversation between Knezevic and Ljuban, but they had an order, and you don't know, however, where that letter came from.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one knows where it could have come from. It couldn't have come from a lower level than the intelligence administration, so it must have come from them, the federal Secretariat, and the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't. I didn't say I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I just wanted to take note of that. Tell me, please. You say on page 4 of your statement that, "After the war in Slovenia, the JNA withdraw to the line that Milosevic had set as the borders of a Greater Serbia." That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. I didn't say that a line that Milosevic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had set but a line imagined by the so-called Rump Yugoslavia or the Greater Serbia, as they called it. And a good part of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look. I'm reading for you. You said that you didn't say it. I didn't make it up. I'm reading from your statement. So let me read it from page 4, the middle of your page 4 of your statement. "Upon the end of the war in Slovenia, the JNA withdrew from there to a line which Milosevic had set as the border of Greater Serbia," et cetera. This is what is stated in your statement. If you didn't say that, tell me.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I said that. I may have made a slip of the tongue. If I did, let me say now that I didn't say that it was Milosevic that had set the borders of Greater Serbia. I don't have that transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not a transcript. It's your statement that you signed, page 4 of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this may be time for the Chamber to have a copy of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we haven't got a copy. Let us have a copy, and let the witness have a copy too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us not waste time. I quoted correctly what is written in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you question a witness about a statement or any other document, he has the right to have it so he can answer, provided it is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, copies for the Chamber will be coming down. I'll just read the whole paragraph, because I'm not suggesting that the sentence wasn't accurately quoted by the accused. It may have been appropriate to put it into context. And in English, particularly in light of an earlier answer and an exchange by the witness and the accused. The paragraph reads: "When the war ended in Slovenia, the JNA pulled out of Slovenia and withdrew to the line that Milosevic had determined was the border for Greater Serbia. This idea of a border for partial Yugoslavia had been written in the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Science. This was Milosevic's goal as it was published, and it was common knowledge that this was Milosevic's plan."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We should have copies for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In the second part, again the same is mentioned as I asked you about. Was it my plan? And you said it wasn't. Now here it says that you're claiming that the memorandum was in fact my plan, Mr. Candic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question. I think you have. I think you have, if you agree. If you agree, I have already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, as a former intelligence officer, inform me too so that I might know. When was it and where did I set or determine the borders of a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, you were given the statement to check.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want me to say when you determined the borders of a Rump Yugoslavia, I will say on this occasion that that was when you took the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, when you became president. Of course, you were the author of the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and in one paragraph of that constitution, it says that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia consists of Serbia and Montenegro and all others who wish to join it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Candic. You remember that in those days we declared very clearly that we had no territorial pretensions towards any of the former Yugoslav republics. But tell me, please, during the time period you're testifying about, which -- of which ethnicities were Admiral Miro Brovet, Grubicic, Jurinovski, Tus, Agotic, Tumanov, et cetera, all these who were in the top military leadership of the Yugoslav People's Army at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain this comment that Serbia or, rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had no pretensions towards other republics, towards the Republic of Croatia and towards Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to the rules of what acts of aggression constitute, a classical act of aggression was committed against both republics with special warfare as an introduction to this. Secondly, when you asked me about the names of certain people and whether I knew them, I did; they are generals. And to be specific, with respect to General Simeon Tumanov, the deputy of General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, chief of the Intelligence Administration, at the end of February or maybe beginning of March, 1992, after the beating by volunteer units in Serbia, I was in hospital at the Military Academy, and I met with General Simeon Tumanov because he had an operation of polyps in his nose. And he told me at the time that I had no reason to abandon the Yugoslav People's Army because Bosnia and Herzegovina would join the Rump Yugoslavia. He used the term "Rump Yugoslavia." So I'm talking about the period I spent at the Military Medical Academy on the 13th floor of the building. And I asked him how, and he said, "With Macedonia, the situation has already been changed," and he, as a Macedonian, had to return to Macedonia, whereas I would have no problems. I should stay in the JNA because Bosnia and Herzegovina would also become a part of the Rump Yugoslavia. I just looked at him and thought to myself that -- actually, I didn't want to make any comments aloud, but I wanted to let him know that he was wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wanted to say that to him, but you didn't?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't tell him that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do I care what you spoke about with a colleague at the Military Academy, he a Macedonian and you a Bosnian? What has that got to do with this?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has plenty to do with the project of creating a Rump Yugoslavia, that is, a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. What you call a Rump Yugoslavia, that is, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which consisted of Serbia and Montenegro, this was the result of the fact that separatist movements in Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Macedonia had separated from Yugoslavia and not because Serbia and Montenegro had seceded from Yugoslavia. That's clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently it's not clear to you that Slovenia was allowed to separate from Yugoslavia because the JNA withdrew in three months instead of within three years, because it had no -- there was no interest in Slovenia for it to remain within Yugoslavia as it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My position is quite the opposite. I think it was in the interest of everyone to preserve Yugoslavia. There was no better country. Unfortunately, the forces who broke it up had other goals in mind. As far as I understand it, you too were for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was, but maybe I don't agree with you when you mention forces. I don't know what you mean when you use the word "forces." I probably have one thing in mind and you something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I mentioned all these high-ranking officers from Admiral Brovet, Ljubicic, Jurinovski, Tus, Agotic, and others. Were they and you thrown out of the JNA? Did anyone throw you out from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct you. Colonel Agotic was not a Serb. He was a Croat. I was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the people I have listed were non-Serbs, and I'm asking you whether they were thrown out of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You too?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not. I threw myself out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who threw these people out of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Imeraj Agotic was thrown out by Colonel Slobodan Rakocevic because he didn't wish to establish any collaborationist position in the leadership of Croatia as an intellectual and a highly educated man, an intelligence officer who headed the security department of the 5th Corps in Zagreb and he was replaced. So he didn't even have an office any more. He went to work and sat with his colleagues in their offices and spent his time there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After so many years, doesn't it seem to you that this so-called idea of a Greater Serbia was simply a screen, a smoke screen, for the achievement of separatist goals in these republics that seceded from Yugoslavia, including Albanian separatism and nationalism?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why it's important what I think. What happened, happened. Of course I don't like most of it. As for assessments and judgements, let time and history have their say about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, something that you must know. In which one of the former republics of the SFRY were there the largest number of national minorities, then and today for that matter? Is it Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Serbia is the republic that had the largest number of national minorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that only in Serbia the national structure from the year 1990 to 2000 did not change? Only in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that a key issue which shook up Serbia was the 1974 constitution and the crisis that set in throughout the former Yugoslavia. The roots of that crisis can be traced to the 1974 constitution because Albanians were given -- Albanians in Kosovo were given autonomy and Vojvodina was granted autonomy. So that Serbia was put in a position to be reduced to Serbia proper, because in the parliament of Serbia, there Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were people from both provinces, and they could out-vote the others when political decisions were taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us not discuss constitutional matters with you but let us refer to your own experience. During your service with the JNA, was a single Hungarian from Vojvodina, a Bulgarian from Eastern Serbia, an Albanian from Kosovo, a Muslim from Sandzak, a Ruthenian or any other national minority member thrown out?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that according to the constitution, Serbia is the state -- a state of all its citizens, that it is defined as such?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that the constitution not of Serbia but of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia says that the -- not the Federal Republic. I'm sorry. Yes, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is a state of the citizens living in it. That is what it is inscribed in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The same is inscribed in the constitution of Serbia, that it is the state of all its citizens?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about the constitution of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what happened after the constitutional solutions and the multi-party elections in Croatia in 1990 regarding the status of the Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that not only Serbs but Muslims, too, in Croatia were reduced to a minority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since your service collected data about the Croatian Ustasha emigres, did you know anything about their plans and ideas with respect to the Yugoslav state?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. As an operative officer in the intelligence service, I did have access to information regarding the activities of hostile Ustasha emigres groups abroad, and all that information pointed to a tendency or, rather, a wish of those emigres, Ustasha emigres circles to create a greater Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that no one then, before that or after that, in Serbia called in question the right of the Croatian people to self-determination but that an ethnically pure Croatia was unacceptable for hundreds of thousands of Serbs who were expelled from there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about an ethnically pure Croatia. I really never heard of any such project nor is there any written trace of that, an ethnically pure Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know of the project that one-third should be converted to Catholicism, one-third expelled, and one-third killed. As an intelligence officer, you knew nothing about that project?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're switching from one subject to another. When talking about the emigres groups or the extremists within those circles did make such statements about the three thirds, as you said, but that was not something that came from the official authorities of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't quote any such things because they're not contained in your statement. Do you know who, among representatives of the extremist Ustasha emigration joined the top level leadership of the Croatian state?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them was Gojko Susak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was Gojko Susak?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gojko Susak, I think, came from Canada to Croatia just before the beginning or, rather, after the multi-party elections and just before the war in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was he in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Defence Minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your statement, I see that you were in charge of the Krajina region. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In charge of what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In charge of the Krajina, that particular region.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't in charge of the Krajina region. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what it says at the beginning of the third paragraph from the top on page 4, and I'll read the whole sentence out to it from the capital letter to the full stop: "I was responsible for the areas of Kosovo and north-eastern Bosnia, but I was also in charge of Krajina." That's what it says in your written statement. I'm asking you now, were you in fact in charge of the Krajina region? You say you weren't.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who wrote this, but let me repeat: I never said that I was in charge of the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Thank you. I'm not going to ask you any more about that because you say yourself that you don't know who wrote your statement.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, possibly it's the translation. I said that I was exclusively in charge of Kosovo and north-eastern Bosnia, but I also said that, according to my official capacity, I travelled both to Croatia and Slovenia and Macedonia and to Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only north-eastern Bosnia but Central Bosnia as well when necessity required or, rather, when I received orders to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you weren't an intelligence officer in Banija, Kordun, Lika; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't in those areas but I said that I was in Bosanska Krajina or, rather, the Bihac area and the airport region in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said that the JNA became an exponent of Serbian policy and this in a strange way, in view of the fact that in 1991 it sent you to Bihac as an officer, and you were a Muslim. So that would appear rather strange. How, then, does that coincide with the statement that you made that it was an exponent of Serb policies?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army as an institutional system didn't send me to Bihac by orders, on orders, but I was sent by orders from colonel Slobodan Rakocevic, and in response to a question I was asked, I explained why he chose me to go. I said he probably trusted me. And the fact that he trusted me testifies to the fact that I was an officer, very conscientious, and it was said in a portion here that for my work and due to my conscientiousness I was promoted to the rank of major of the air force before my time within the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that. That just proves that there was no discrimination but that you were favoured and that you were judged according to the results of your labours.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I said that during my testimony today. I said there was no discrimination towards me personally, that I felt no pressure exerted upon me, and that people right up to 1987 and even 1988 and 1989 and 1990 were ranked according to their abilities, the results of their labour, and not according to their national or ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, then. So when they sent you on that assignment, did you fulfil your assignment? Did you find the transmitter you were sent to find?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in finding transmitters. I was just sent there to take through a column of three radio reconnaissance vehicles with their crews on board, and that's why I stayed there for three or four days, because I was waiting for these teams, for those crews, to find the transmitter. Whether they actually found it or not, I don't know, because they were supposed to hand in their reports to their superiors. It wasn't within my mandate to look into the affair myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Tell me this: After the event that you describe when you say that because of the shooting that took place on some of the reservists that some bombs were thrown in a village but you don't remember the name of the village, whether it was Zegar or Vaganac, which of those two villages, and you go on to say that you saw that the village had been set alight. Now, do you know whether anybody was killed on that occasion during that operation, how many people were killed, what happened at all?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to speak about that in detail, but when I went to Bihac, I noticed enormous flames and smoke. And when I arrived at the airport in Bihac, I met Colonel Topalovic, Jovo Topalovic, who screamed at me and who was swearing, who cursed all the generals in Belgrade and asked me, "What's that you're doing over there, because the whole village has been torched." The whole airport is on its feet, and so is the air force and with bombs, inflammatory bombs launched on the villages. The villages were set alight, and I don't know how many people were killed. But I did see, judging by the reactions of the colonel, Colonel Jovan Topalovic who replaced Igor Topalovic as head of security of the 5th Air Force Corps, that he was dissatisfied, because he said that this was all rigged and that somebody had purposely fired at the paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Candic, we will get on better if you try and concentrate on the question. In the middle of that you said you don't know how many people were killed. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know which village that actually was; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was saying you don't know which village it was.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vaganac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know if there are any dead, any people killed, and you don't know who gave the orders for the village to be bombed in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what Colonel Topalovic told me, the order for the aeroplanes to leave Bihac airport with the incendiary bombs, the orders were issued by the commander of the air force brigade, Mahmut Skadrac [phoen] and Slobodan Jeremic, who was at the Bihac airport very frequently as head of air support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was this brigade commander by way of ethnicity? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was from a mixed marriage, the child of a mixed marriage. I don't know whether his father was a Serb or his mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Mahmud.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see, Mahmud. Right. Now, as you said that you came -- you saw the officers drinking and celebrating in the mess; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me, what mess was this that served alcohol to the officers?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the military canteens, there is no alcoholic beverage, but on that particular night in the canteen or restaurant or mess where the pilots take their meals, there was alcoholic beverage, more than in any other restaurant, I would say, which generally served alcoholic beverages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me the name of one -- at least one officer who was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were Cako Ivan, Baraban Mirko; people from my own class and group, year, those two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say you met Cedomir Knezevic; right? That's what it says in your statement. What was the reason for this meeting of yours?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reason was because I was supposed to wait for three or four days, to stay at the airport, sleep there, in order to escort the column back to Belgrade. And as I saw that Jovan Topalovic was drunk, I knew that I couldn't sit down and talk to him but I was on good terms with Cedo, and I asked him where Cedo Knezevic was, although I knew he was at the Bihac airport, and he said he was at the hunting lodge. And he took me to the hunting lodge, in fact, which is where I set up my accommodation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The weapons that the JNA gave out to the JNA, was it from the JNA depots or from the Territorial Defence depots?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying for the umpteenth time that the weapons were from the TO depots of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, why in this action to arm Serbs in Croatia, why would the Croats themselves take part? Could you explain that absurdity? Because you say that Miroslav Jarun, a Croat, was a participant in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say Miroslav Jarun but Miroslav Juran.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right Juran then.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Juran was not in Bihac. Miroslav Juran was stationed in Dvor Na Uni, together with Slavuj Ljubisa, and he did not take part in the handing out of weapons. It was Major Cedo Knezevic who was in the hunting lodge which is where the depots and stockpiles were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he was engaged in this operation. He was part of it, according to what you say, right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Juran was a member of the 2nd Detachment of the counter-intelligence group from Zagreb, and they had moved because they were afraid of being arrested, so they had displaced and moved to Bihac. Part of them were in Bihac and another part in Dvor Na Uni, and the third part of the detachment had moved to Glina or rather, Petrinja. And every one of them had the task of developing a network, which meant that the collaborators in Glina, Dvor Na Uni, Bosanski Novi formed this network of collaborators and informers within the frameworks of Proboj 1 and the dissemination of weapons to Serbs in Krajina Lika and Kordun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, but everything that you know about Proboj 1, that particular operation, you learned from Knezevic, as far as I was able to gather, right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and saw it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With your own eyes. You said you saw a report with your own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the weapons and when the weapons were taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inform your superiors about everything you had learnt?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't inform anybody. That was not my assignment or mission. I was just there on assignment, that is to say, to wait for those who had gone there to find the radio ham transmitters and take them back to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said you would see on a daily basis at least three or four trucks loaded full of weapons which where driven by regular JNA soldiers, escorted by the military police, as they left the depots and warehouses. That's what it says on page 6, paragraph 4 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the statement is now available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite possibly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We're going to give this an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 350, tab 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I go ahead with my question now, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you say on page 6, paragraph 4, is the following: "Every day I saw at least three or four trucks loaded with weapons," et cetera, et cetera, "leave the warehouse." Now, my question for you is why, then, on page 5, in paragraph 5, you claim the following, and I quote: "Those weapons were not being smuggled to Serb civilians but representatives of the Serbs would come with a list of individuals that supported the Serb rebellion and who should be armed. The Serbs were coming to Bihac in their own trucks to pick up weapons for their villages." Now, which of those two statements is correct, Mr. Candic? Which of those two claims?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that every day three to four trucks were parked in the vicinity on the plateau near the hunting lodge. I said that I had occasion to see, one day, how two trucks were driven off when the representatives of the Serbs turned up, those who had come to ask for what they needed. I didn't say that this happened every day. Perhaps there was a slip during the translation. I didn't say that every day I saw at least three to four trucks being driven off. But when it came to smuggling, I did say that Major Cedo Knezevic told me that if he learnt that any one of the Serbs who had been given weapons, that he would have shot them personally. So I don't know who did the translation of this, but that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as the translation is concerned, the translators here are very good. So those arguments that you put forward and people put forward very frequently, I've heard them umpteen times. Let me just remind you what it says in your statement. "Every day," it says, "I saw at least three or four trucks loaded with weapons leave the warehouse." Now you say that one day you happened to see two trucks parked by there somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I saw them parked. I said I saw them loaded and that they were driven off with the weapons. That's what I said just now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how did you know where those trucks were going and who was taking over the weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I knew where they were going, where their destination was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in Bihac -- when you were in Bihac, did you contact anybody else except Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Slobodan Jeremic was there all the time. For those three or four days that I was there, he was there too, and I can see that he was involved in this whole situation, that he knew everything about it, and Slobodan Jeremic, Colonel Slobodan Jeremic, head of the air force support from Zemun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me now, please, when you're talking about the two trucks loaded up with weapons who arrived at the headquarters in Zemun, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that Rakocevic protested. So he couldn't have been the organiser of the Proboj 1 operation, or perhaps the Proboj 1 operation was an operation contrary to the smuggling of weapons. Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which is correct. I said that Rakocevic did lodge protests and said why things were going on without his knowing about it. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But later on, you say that he issued the order for the weapons to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. He said that the weapons could be distributed only to those people who deserved to be given one artillery piece and a maximum of ten barrels, which is what Major Karan obtained from the entire contingent and handed over to those people in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means those ten barrels, that was actually the Operation Proboj 2. That was the whole operation, was it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say those ten barrels were the Proboj 2 operation, because later on in my statement I go on to say that Major Ljuban Karan turned towards Goran Hadzic more and more often and that he would go to Novi Sad frequently and approach the security service and Arkan there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you said that as a result of this operation, you said a moment -- a few days ago, seven or eight pieces handed over to friends. Now you say ten. Let it be ten.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said ten at the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. So that's what the Proboj 2 operation means. That's what you know about it; right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So these seven or eight artillery pieces were distributed to friends, right, to their associates by way of a gift?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to associates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, to associates. Can you then refer to this as arming the Serbs, use the term "arming the Serbs" if that's what it was?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it was arming the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Candic. On page 8, paragraph 4, you say that the images and footage of massacred civilians came in who were killed by Croatian paramilitary formations. However, you were of the opinion that those civilians were actually killed by the Serbs. Now, why did you think that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained that today in the first portion of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained that it wasn't logical to you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, right. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have no actual knowledge about that. All you said was that it didn't seem logical to you if civilians were massacred and then the people who massacred withdrew and then these other people found them, took footage of them, and that it wasn't logical for those who did that to take the bodies off.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's illogical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's illogical only because they left them lying there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are more reasons why it seemed illogical but I wouldn't like to lecture anyone here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You claim that something like that could not have happened to Croat paramilitary formations, nothing like the killing and mutilating of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have happened once or twice but it couldn't have been happening all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're drawing to an end. You've got another two minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have quite a few questions left, Mr. May. I really don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were given extensive time. I'll give you another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be extremely difficult to choose from these, because I've got about 50 questions left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, is it true that during your service, your tour of duty in Tuzla, you monitored the arming of paramilitary formations such as the Green Berets and the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my statement that I monitored the arming of all three ethnic groups. I didn't say a single word about the Green Berets or the Patriotic League. Of course, if I have the opportunity to say so now, I know for certain that in north-eastern Bosnia, there were no Green Berets or any formations of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Vahid Karavelic is?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that he was a captain of the JNA at that time, commander of the Patriotic League for north-eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic was arrested in Zivinice in north-eastern Bosnia and taken to Sremska Mitrovica to prison. He was later exchanged. It is true he was a captain of the Yugoslav People's Army. His assignment was to coordinate the Patriotic League, but it was only coordination. No operation involving arming or organisation of paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you claim there were no paramilitary formations of the Patriotic League in north-eastern Bosnia, and now you say that Captain Karavelic was commander -- was coordinator of the Patriotic League. I call him commander, you call him coordinator. What is true?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying he was not the commander of the Patriotic League, but he was involved with people who were members of the Patriotic League, and one of them was Haris Redzic. He was the one who sheltered Captain Vahid Karavelic, and Karavelic even lived at his place for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that he blocked the supply of food to units near a military airport?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that during an operation which you commanded directly, you had a conflict with Karavelic's people and a lieutenant of the JNA, an Albanian, was killed then?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who was killed. Raif -- first of all, I didn't command any operation. But when Lieutenant Raif Miftari was killed, I was in Belgrade. I learnt about it later. I learnt that he was killed near Zivinice, by his own commander, by the way, the commander of the artillery and rockets regiment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you arrested Karavelic himself and transported him to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica by helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just told you, didn't I, that I never saw Vahid Karavelic in north-eastern Bosnia. I couldn't have transported him via helicopter. I'm not a pilot. I couldn't have done it myself. I wasn't even there when not only he but two other people were arrested and taken to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mitrovica is not in north-eastern Bosnia. Is it true that his -- that documents concerning the arming of the 108th Brigade of the ZNG, the Croatian National Guard, were found on him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information you had thanks to your rank and position, is it true that you gave them to another intelligence service after leaving the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the information I had access to thanks to my rank and position was indeed given by me not to intelligence services but to one intelligence service, sorry, the service for the protection of the constitutional order of the Republic of Croatia. Radenko Radojcic was the person I gave them to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you join the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was commander of the municipal -- Territorial Defence headquarters for the Brcko municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that after leaving the JNA, you spent some time in Italy and Austria?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while I did live in Austria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you contact any foreign intelligence services there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this must be your last question now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have many questions unasked left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Fikret Muslimovic is?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fikret Muslimovic is an officer from the security service of the former JNA, and during the aggression committed against Bosnia and Herzegovina, he was an officer of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that as an intelligence officer, he was in charge of monitoring the nationalism in the religious orders of the Catholics and that -- and Catholic clergies?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was never a member of the counter-intelligence group. Within his purview, on his job in the unit, he could have monitored the clergies, emigres groups, but only within the unit. But -- and he could have recruited moles only from the people within the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Milosevic, you've had your time. Yes. Does the amicus have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I do have a number of questions. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order not to come back to it later, since Mr. Candic said a lot of things today, I would ask him to clarify a couple of points. First of all, the recent questions concerning the tapes of massacred civilians. He already gave us his own explanation. However, in your statement, Mr. Candic, I mean the witness statement, page 9, paragraph 2 in the English version, three last sentences, and in your statement you have in front of you it's page 8, paragraph 4, you say you were never quite certain what these people's ethnicity was. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I wasn't prepared to accept this information for granted, although it was alleged by Katancic and Karan they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were not sure of their ethnicity is what you said. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were no inscriptions. There was no writing or sign anywhere on their body parts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking if that's what you said. I was pointing out something illogical about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you say in this statement, since it is already exhibited here, otherwise I wouldn't be using it probably, you mentioned this officer or soldier who executed four persons by shooting them in the back. How come you never mentioned it during any of the previous interviews? Because it is a gruesome incident.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me earlier. I mentioned it today because I was asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw that Radojcic Radenko doing nothing to punish this officer or soldier who did this, why didn't you report it to some of your superior officers or the military prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a junior to Colonel Radojcic Radenko, rather, Lieutenant Colonel Radojcic Radenko who was head of the counter-intelligence group, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but I did have a verbal duel with him on the subject. However, I did not think it was my job or my duty to report it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were talking about Opera and Labrador, you mentioned wire taps and intercepts. Did this group, including you in that service, engage primarily in operations that were designed to prevent the break-up of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was talking about Opera, its main objective was propaganda operations designed to influence the psychology, the mind-set, beliefs of people in those places where this information was presented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that it was organised that 70 aeroplanes should cross over to the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the military prosecutor of the JNA had them all arrested in 1992 for precisely this?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened then. I left the army in 1992. I am not aware of what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yourself that they were all arrested.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who was arrested?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Vasiljevic, Rakocevic and the Opera group were arrested rather than 70 pilots who were preparing to desert with their aeroplanes to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understood you as saying that this group was arrested, as suggested by the military prosecutor of the JNA, and brought to justice.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a trial. I was even a witness. And what I said today, including what I said about those two trucks and weapons and the work of the Opera I said on that occasion in Belgrade as well, and I suppose there must be transcripts of my testimony there. I didn't know I would end up here today, telling the same story. I said what I knew as a witness in Zagreb in the case against Radenko Radojcic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you only to answer my questions rather than give me elaborate explanations. I'm only asking you were they were arrested or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have three subjects to cover, Your Honours, related to this witness's testimony. First of all, on Day One you spoke about the fact that the army penetrated civilian structures in 1989, 1990, and 1991.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say the army penetrated them. I said members of counter-intelligence groups created moles or collaborator positions in civilian structures in these years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was it possible for someone to work for 30 years in your organisation, named KOG, without knowing that it was called "KOG" rather than "KOS"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever in the structure where I worked used the term "KOS." They always said "KOG."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could anyone have been a mole or an informer for KOG without knowing it was called KOG?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody is a collaborator, he is run by one operative officer. He is not even supposed to know where that officer works.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he is aware only of this one individual. He doesn't know anything about other employees of the KOG.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in those civilian structures, you conducted investigations. You monitored people. You conducted surveillance.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only received reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You only collected data, information about those people?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Judges, I would like you to give me a few explanations. The army consists mainly of professionals, officers and NCOs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army consists of two components: The armed forces, that is the Yugoslav People's Army, which includes the active-duty force, officers, NCOs and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in this second segment, soldiers. How many soldiers were full-time employed in the JNA, or is it true that 70 per cent of the JNA consisted of conscripts who served their military duty?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody served for 12 months.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 90 to 95 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were conscripts?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before coming to serve in the army, they were civilians, and when they finished, they became civilians again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've come to the time when we must adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Candic, could you please answer my questions with a yes or no or as briefly as possible. We came to the point when civilians, citizens between 18 and 20 years of age, would spend up to a year in the army, upon which they would return to civilian life; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When doing their military service, was the principle that a Croat should serve in Serbia, a Macedonian in Slovenia, a Serb in Slovenia, a Montenegrin in Bosnia; was that the principle applied?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no special principle or key as to where recruits would be assigned to do their military service, but in any event, efforts were made that he shouldn't serve close to his home but further away, and as a rule, in another republic of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So in view of that, I'm asking you as an officer, and especially since you're familiar with life in the army, could any nation living in Yugoslavia feel that it was being occupied by another nation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an officer, I can say that I could never discover any elements of one nation occupying another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And was one of the main duties of the officers to develop tolerance, absolute tolerance of different religions and ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this apply to the officers as well?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The army, up to 1989, did it interfere at all in civilian affairs except in humanitarian campaigns?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army interfered in civilian affairs, as I tried to explain, when it came to operations of a federal level, if we're talking about the security segment, when both JNA security services and the State Security Service would participate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period of some 50 years or 40 to 50 years. Is it true to say that the army interfered in civilian affairs only in the case of elemental disasters, the building of bridges and roads, and no other civilian affairs?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, it did not interfere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Another point has to do with everything that you said with respect to the memorandum in Serbia. You may be right, I'm not absolutely familiar with this subject matter, but I think that you are right when you said that it was first published in 1986, and I think it was in a newspaper called Vecernje Novosti, an evening paper.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in which newspaper it was published, but the memorandum as a document as such existed. It wasn't published in the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that this document ever acquired an official form signed by its -- the people who drafted it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that it was by the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're claiming that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us with respect to 1986 what state positions did Milosevic hold, Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1986, I think he was president of the League of Communists of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any position in the state administration?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday or, rather, not yesterday but during your examination-in-chief, though you denied it a moment ago, I have in front of me the French version of the transcript from the hearing during your examination-in-chief, and you said, the page 12701 in the French version, I think it coincides with the English version, when you said that the main initiator of this project called the memorandum was Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried on a number of occasions to say that he was not the creator of that document, but he was the person who had it carried out, implemented, that he was the key figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm asking you something else. If you say that he was the initiator, that would mean that he initiated or prompted the Academy of Sciences to compile such a document.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I think it was the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. 12702, line 10, I have to read it out in French so as not to make any mistakes, so could the -- "He saw in the memorandum and what Slobodan Milosevic was about to do, the disintegration of Yugoslavia, of that Yugoslavia, and the establishment of a Greater Serbia project." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Is that what it says in the memorandum?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say in the memorandum. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're claiming that the memorandum deals with the disintegration of Yugoslavia and that that in fact was the desire of Milosevic in the days when the memorandum was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that it was the wish of Milosevic. And the question that you quoted from the memorandum referred to the position of the Serbs as the most numerous nation in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also say in your statement, page 4, paragraph 9 of the English version, "According to that idea on the borders of a Rump Yugoslavia is referred to in the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Sciences." Does that memorandum indeed speak about those borders if you claim that you have read the memorandum?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the position of the Serbian nation is addressed, one can infer from that which part or which territories inhabited by Serbs should belong to the most numerous nation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the memorandum speaks about the disintegration of Yugoslavia. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the memorandum, it says that the thesis should be overcome according to which a weak Serbia implies a strong Yugoslavia. So in other words, one needs to break up Yugoslavia to strengthen Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is your interpretation, but does it say that explicitly in the memorandum?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The third topic I would like to address, and I think that will be my last, you said that after Slovenia and Croatia, you realised that the JNA had sided with one ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether Slovenia in those days really was a republic in Yugoslavia with a higher standard of living and where there were no ethnic tensions?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The standard of living was the highest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true there were no ethnic tensions in that republic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no ethnic tensions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that you referred to the memorandum as a member of this service you belonged to, do you know anything about the events linked to Mladina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you did, this happened in 1988, wasn't it? Wasn't the idea launched by Mladina that the military service should be done as civilians? In other words, that the country should be demilitarised then disarmed, and the expenses for the JNA, the budget reduced? One of the main advocates of that was Janez Jansa.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he later become Defence Minister in the days when disarmament was advocated? Was -- were people disarmed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were weapons distributed to them at one point in time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point when border posts needed to be taken control of in 1991 in Slovenia, when the conflict broke out in Slovenia, then individuals broke into warehouses and seized weapons from TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The barracks were surrounded in Slovenia, and attack was launched against the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is rather a broad topic, and one shouldn't go into it whether they were surrounded. Yes, they were surrounded. As to the scenario and who had arranged what, I had my own opinion about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that over a period of ten days - there were no conflicts anywhere yet - in Slovenia between 40 and 50 young men were killed after they had raised their hands in surrender?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the figure of the number of killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As your service, did you see a film, a footage that was shown when about 40 young men between 18 and 20 years of age are standing with their hands up and they're being fired at and killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as an individual, call the conflict in Slovenia as a show, as a film type of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, those boys had surrendered. They didn't want to engage in conflict.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After all that, the Presidency of Slovenia called this an aggression by the JNA against independent Slovenia and called on the population to resist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Our time is limited, and I'm not sure this witness is in the best position to deal with these matters even if relevant. Yes. Have you finished now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge May, I am -- I'll finish in a second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that after this clash in Slovenia, what happened in Slovenia, it was only after that that Proboj 1, 2, and 3 took place. In October. This was in June when these soldiers were killed and Proboj 1, 2, and 3, occurred in October 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, explain then, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Proboj 1, I learnt of Proboj 1 sometime in September, and from the document that was shown here, one could see that Lieutenant Colonel Smiljanic conducted that Operation Proboj 1 even in July, which means before the war broke out in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about Proboj 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proboj 2 was a continuation in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, these three operations, Proboj 1, 2, and 3, were they after the events in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were before October 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then your statement earlier on is not correct, because in your testimony, you referred to October up to December.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is when I learnt about them, but they started earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, the arming didn't occur after the memorandum.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The memorandum was in 1986.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any arming then?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think there are three passages in the statement that I will take with you first of all. And the Chamber will have noticed that the page numbering is different in the version that you have and the version that I think the accused has, but I'll deal with the version the Chamber has. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the foot of page 4, the accused suggested in a question that the witness had acknowledged responsibility for events in the Krajina. In fact what he said is as follows, and perhaps you can just listen to this, Mr. Candic, and confirm that this is correct: "My responsibilities were the areas of Kosovo and north-eastern Bosnia, however, I did have assignments to the Krajina." Does that adequately reflect your position? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just explain what your position was in relation to the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position in relation to Krajina was not such that I had any kind of participation or any kind of assignments or obligations there. As a member of the Central Counter-Intelligence Group, I wanted to explain to Their Honours that I frequently took part in the final stages of operations in Zagreb, in Sarajevo, Tuzla. So independently of my two zones of responsibilities for -- of which I was in charge. That is what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 7, at the foot. Mr. Tapuskovic suggested there was no reference in your earlier statements to the execution of four Croat civilians. The last paragraph, the Chamber will see that it is indeed there. Page 9, please. As to Proboj 2, Mr. Candic, and the possibility of the filmed bodies being of uncertain ethnicity, you say in your witness statement the following: "That the civilians filmed -" that's the dead civilians filmed - "were from the villages of Nustar, Borovo Naselje, Vinkovci, and the railway centre at Osijek." Can you, one by one, just tell us what your understanding of the ethnic composition or domination of those locations is, if you know.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, half/half, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few other questions in reverse order. You were asked by Mr. Tapuskovic about people working for intelligence services, and you explained how such people weren't supposed to know even where the operative works. Two questions, please. You were involved in counter-intelligence. Were you aware - yes or no - of active intelligence agencies or services, the sort of agencies that might have included work abroad?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the body for which you worked have such an active intelligence element to it or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The body that I worked for, the sector for foreign intelligence services and the immigration sector did have collaborators abroad, and sometimes those people went to attend meetings abroad and to receive reports from their agents there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
